items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received

Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials

Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to.…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Google’s Embrace of AI Is Backfiring Spectacularly: It turns out that forcing its users to read AI answers is bad news for Google's lucrative ad business.
items.content:
Google’s pivot to AI is unloading a machine gun into its foot.

Its rapid of embrace of AI features, which it’s obnoxiously infused into the very top of its popular search engine, is blowing back on its lucrative advertising business. When there’s a Google AI Overview giving users the answer they’re looking for, there’s no need for them to scroll down to search through links where the ads are displayed.

The bottom line is fewer users are are actually seeing the ads and clicking on them. And, importantly, fewer business customers willing to pay to show ads on the platform, as their potential customers spend time arguing with Google’s AI Mode instead of visiting their websites.

“What we’re seeing is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior,” Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at the marketing agency VML, told the New York Times .

Marshall Evans, a marketer who helps small businesses put up ads on Google Search, complained to the newspaper that “AI takes over such a large amount of the search results now.”

In one illustrative example, Evans said he was spending just $500 per month on search ads for one of his clients, compared to $2,000 per month a year ago. Now he’s using the dough to advertise on streaming platforms like Tubi and platforms like Reddit instead, making it an all the more stinging blow for the tech colossus. It’s not that people aren’t willing to pay for advertising anymore; they’re just not willing to pay for it on the AI-dominated landscape that Google has turned its search engine into.

“Google is trying to take a business that was the best business in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business that doesn’t have the same advantages,” Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, told the NYT . “Making that transition is a lot harder than Google’s management thought it would be.”

The tech giant’s recent Q3 earnings report painted a grim picture. For the first time ever, it reported that its search advertising revenue had fallen to less than 50 percent of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue, the NYT noted.

Its growth of revenue from search also showed signs of tapering off , dipping from a 14.5 year-over-year increase to a 12 percent year-over-year increase. That’s despite Google saying its search engine was fielding more queries than ever. Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler spelled it out by admitting that the disappointing growth was because of “lower monetization we’re seeing in AI mode.”

In sum, Google can be said to have taken a “shoot first, as questions about advertising later” approach to AI. And with its cash cow starting to falter, now it’s time to start asking those questions.

items.title: This Week in Plasma: CJK Text Input and Performance
items.content:
This Week in Plasma: CJK Text Input and Performance

Welcome to a new issue of This Week in Plasma!

Plasma’s on-screen keyboard now includes various text composers for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. (Devin Lin, plasma-keyboard MR #113 )

You can now control the rate at which the text insertion point blinks throughout most apps, or make it stop blinking entirely. (Alexander Berg, KDE Bugzilla #343635 )

The Kicker Application Menu widget now supports showing a text label alongside the icon, just like Kickoff does. (小太, KDE Bugzilla #456252 )

KRunner’s window is no longer so flickery and jumpy as it grows and shrinks. (Victor Prudniy, KDE Bugzilla #513950 )

The Networks widget no longer offers you the opportunity to connect to a Wi-Fi network via a QR code on systems with no Wi-Fi adapters. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #517252 )

It’s now possible to play or pause media on the lock screen using a device that sends explicit “play” or “pause” signals, not just the combined “play/pause” toggle. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #500388 )

The Kickoff Application Launcher widget now displays more standard behavior for the highlighting applied to its grid items after you right-click them. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #505920 )

On a multi-screen setup, right-clicking the desktop and choosing “Display Configuration” now opens the relevant System Settings page showing the screen with the desktop you right-clicked. (Kai Uwe Broulik and Joshua Goins, kscreen MR #522 )

System Settings’ Accessibility page now includes convenient links to pages where you can change the display scale or font sizes. (Alexander Berg, KDE Bugzilla #462501 )

System Settings’ Font Management page has been transformed into a standalone app. It seemed to fit better that way, and this reduces the clutter in System Settings. (Tobias Fella, plasma-workspace MR #7395 )

The indicator highlight for panel widgets with a popup open is now sized in the same way that it is for System Tray widgets, improving consistency. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #522844 )

Synchronizing your Plasma desktop settings to Plasma Login Manager now includes your Night Light settings, too. (Anton Birkel, KDE Bugzilla #521408 )

Deleting a panel now deletes any global shortcuts that had been assigned to its widgets, preventing them from forever cluttering up System Settings’ Shortcuts page and your Plasma config file. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #410903 )

The Web Browser widget’s custom home page setting now works. (Christoph Wolk, kdeplasma-addons MR #1286 )

Fixed a bug that prevented connecting to an OpenConnect VPN with authentication group names in Chinese. (Zheng Ender, plasma-nm MR #698 )

Fixed a recent regression that made KWin crash at login on certain systems. (Xaver Hugl, KDE Bugzilla #528824 )

Fixed a case where KWin could crash after a GPU reset. (Xaver Hugl, kwin MR #10349 )

Fixed a case where Plasma could crash when you unplugged a removable USB disk very quickly after telling Plasma to safely eject it. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #526537 )

Fixed a case where Plasma could crash when you removed a Weather Report widget. (Bohdan Onofriichuk, KDE Bugzilla #528997 )

Fixed a case where notifications about your battery being critically low could pile up after waking the computer. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #520491 )

When Plasma is woken up due to certain kinds of background network and Bluetooth activity, now it goes to sleep again afterwards. (Michael Auer, powerdevil MR #706 )

Fixed a case where Discover would fail to install local package files (e.g. .rpm or .deb files) when the PackageKit daemon wasn’t already running. (Taras Oleksyn, KDE Bugzilla #528037 )

The “Horizontal Bars” display style for System Monitor sensors now looks correct when using a left-to-right language like Arabic or Hebrew. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #523137 )

Pressing keys on your keyboard’s numberpad no longer activates KRunner when they aren’t supposed to.…

items.title: Inkling 2 Mini
items.content:
Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

Reported coding scores for models under 100B total parameters. The green line is the frontier with Inkling 2 Mini, the dashed line the frontier without it, and the shading the ground it adds. Decoding speed is a theoretical ceiling at 614 GB/s with BF16 weights and batch size one, including repeated reads across loops. Evaluation setups vary by model.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB) Airplane mode

Open video: PlaneBench flight simulator demo, screen with phone video inset

Loading the flight simulator Inkling 2 Mini built… To try the flight simulator, open this page on desktop.

Building and flying a flight simulator with Inkling 2 Mini. The timer shows real time; most of the recording plays at 15× speed.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model , we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and…

items.title: Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu
items.content:
I’m pleased to announce a new source control tool, jj-musubi , that

live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu ( jj ) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj

snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases,

This simple capability is surprisingly powerful.

I often work on one machine, and build or test on others. Now they get my changes as I make

them, and I don’t need to remember whether I was editing on my laptop or someplace else.

If I fetch changes from or push changes to upstream, all of my copies stay up to date.

jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).

It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security

model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).

Jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of

my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my

shell prompt run jj status , so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots.

jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and

workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in new history while

a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my

machine will sync when I’m back on the network.

This has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent

its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop

to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can

coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead.

jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive .

I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to

lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets

forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter

Back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s

Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google

engineers have something similar with an internal jj server.

Since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I

could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub,

and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get.

What’s tricky is getting concurrent work right . That’s already hard in any distributed source

control system, and when syncs are live and we plan for disconnected work in an unreliable

As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exactly I can safely close my laptop after

finishing an edit; all of my changes should make it through either just before I close it, or

right after I reopen. No work should get lost or corrupted in the presence of interrupts,

resends, delays, or machines sleeping, and the system should stay reliable even when machines go

I used Lean to prove key properties of jj-musubi’s network protocol, and tests compare the Rust

code against that model. An extensive body of other tests run real jj repositories through

concurrent edits, interrupted syncs, hub restarts, and a myriad of other nasty situations.

Mutation and adversarial testing ensure that when bugs are injected, sensible things happen. The

safety guide details all the checks (and the parts I don’t yet cover).

It might sound spooky or dangerous to be able to see in-progress work on one machine from

If you use jj in multiple workspaces, you’re already used to the novelty of being able to check

out the same change in two workspaces and modify it. jj simply marks the change as divergent,

but it won’t update either…

items.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
items.content:
Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao

Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:

See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

David Hilbert in 2443: Has someone proved the Riemann Hypothesis?

Thank you for the ordering by how digested the results are. That ordering is the whole story, and it is worth being explicit about why.

For the first two results the digestion path is already visible: human-readable proof, strategy broadly clear, Lean formalisation on top. A reader can form a judgement in an afternoon. The third has no such path yet. A Lean-only artifact of that size is a different kind of object, and the question “is it right” splits into questions that resolve on very different timescales: does the headline statement in Lean say what we mean by GRH; does the archive compile against a known-good Lean with only standard axioms; is the strategy something a number theorist recognises as a proof. The Zulip thread can answer the second relatively quickly. The third is the one that has always taken years.

The two precedents are both uncomfortable. Wiles announced in 1993, the gap surfaced within months, and the repair took until 1995. Mochizuki published in a refereed journal in 2012 and the people who work on the problem still do not accept it. In neither case could the answer be read off the artifact.

Which makes the interesting question not “is it true” but “what observable event would settle it, and who is entitled to say so”. For anyone trying to price this rather than just follow it, writing that down before the claim exists is the only version that is worth anything. Written afterwards it collapses into an argument about credibility, which is precisely the failure mode this whole episode is about.

Disclosure: I work on https://science.markets , which runs a market on this question. The resolution rule is fixed before the market opens and cannot be edited: https://science.markets/markets/riemann-zeta-critical-line/ — it requires a complete unconditional proof in ZFC, independently checked with no unresolved gap, and it says in advance that finite numerical verification does not count and that independence from ZFC leaves it unresolved. Being forced to write down what does not count was the useful part.

Perhaps the world has changed in the last 2.5 months, however, I cannot help but remember your warning in early September,

“The point remains that there is a substantial opportunity cost in converting a historically productive and motivating problem (such as Navier-Stokes regularity) into a mere viral social media post advertising some benchmark progress, rather than actually advancing the field and developing the next generation of both problems to ask, and people to work on them.”

It feels like Alpöge’s actions around GRH have seen your fears come to fruition. I cannot help but feel that regardless of our feelings around the use of AI in mathematics we as a math community should not highlight Alpöge’s actions without a healthy dose of criticism.

If something is lean verified I think releasing is a good thing. The community can begin digesting/interpreting or building off of the results more quickly and with great plurality.

Also, if an individual withholds new results because they feel they have greater results upcoming, that’s well within their right, of course that comes at a risk.

Ideally well known vehicles will emerge for triaging huge lean results, and another vehicle that is meant for human consumption.

items.content:
Subscribers to LWN.net made this article — and everything that

surrounds it — possible. If you appreciate our content, please

The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation

Binder driver , the primary interprocess communication mechanism

used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C

code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into

replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust

implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most

difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas said, as an interprocess

communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in

it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for

allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also,

therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained

attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas

explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive

security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in

the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

That made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas said. Binder was the first user

of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not

of what became the Rust implementation until 2023 , well after the Rust experiment started

in 2021. All told, the effort took more than

five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check,

and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion

devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions

per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the

interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version

would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

One particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput

doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most

screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the

frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a

real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once

in a while, people will notice and care.

The actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she

continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust

handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency

from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported

traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another

process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty

milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

It was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved

as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able

to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent

lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: " I deviated from C

Binder, and pow . It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks. "

Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases.

And the C implementation was still producing new vulnerabilities every time

someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to

only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to

switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has

resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version,

because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the

items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.

AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply

Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers

The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs

Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits

JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.

One of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.

JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.

Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.

Baseline JEDEC Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s)

Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s)

Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.

Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.

At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.

DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).

items.content:
An experimental Android compatibility layer for macOS, Linux, and the browser.

Inspired by Wine: run Android APKs without booting an Android OS.

Written in Rust, WineDroid executes DEX bytecode, implements Android framework

behavior, and renders app interfaces with Skia. Desktop builds include a

Cranelift JIT. The WebAssembly build runs the same runtime and renderer in your

Very early development. Some apps and workflows run; compatibility is

limited. Expect missing APIs and broken apps.

See the individual reports for what works and what doesn't, and the

Install a recent stable Rust toolchain and native C/C++ build tools. On macOS,

use Xcode Command Line Tools. On Linux, also install pkg-config and the

FreeType and Fontconfig development packages; running the desktop app requires

git clone https://github.com/sohzm/winedroid.git

cargo build --release --locked --bin winedroid

./target/release/winedroid /path/to/app.apk

App data lives in ~/.winedroid/default . Set WINEDROID_PREFIX to use another

directory. See usage for package management, display settings,

With Emscripten's emcc on your PATH and Python 3 installed:

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-emscripten

python3 -m http.server 4173 --directory web

Open localhost:4173 and choose or drop an APK. App data

is lost on reload. The browser build does not support Android native .so

Development is intermittent. Contributions and reproducible bug reports are

welcome. Include the app version, host OS, steps to reproduce, and error output.

Read the architecture and contributor instructions

before changing runtime behavior. Compatibility fixes should implement Android

primitives that benefit other apps too. The validation gate is

scripts/validate.sh ; benchmark APK setup is described in AGENTS.md .

GPLv3 only . Third-party components retain their respective licenses;

Execution is best-effort by default. When a guest method call reaches explicitly

reported missing support, winedroid prints FIXME with the primitive identity,

then substitutes void, numeric zero (including false),

or null according to the return type. Existing side effects are not rolled back.

This helps discover multiple missing primitives in one run; output after a

substitution is not evidence of Android compatibility. Guest exceptions and

unrelated runtime failures still propagate, and missing objects can cause later

An interrupted caller is reported as CONTEXT: abandoned ...; caused by: ...

and grouped under the underlying primitive in the report, rather than counted

as a separate missing API. This relationship comes from the error being handled.

Substituted values are not tracked through later execution, so subsequent null

errors are not automatically attributed to an earlier missing call.

Use WINEDROID_STRICT=1 cargo run -- /path/to/app.apk to stop on missing support.

scripts/validate.sh forces strict mode. For direct conformance runs, use

WINEDROID_STRICT=1 cargo test --offline .

primitive identities, hit counts and first context. It is updated as discoveries

occur, so a later abnormal exit does not lose earlier reports. FIXME output is

emitted on first discovery, with an incomplete-execution summary at normal exit.

Normal launches print a short header with runtime and app versions, host,

execution mode and start time. After that, missing support is reported once per

primitive as FIXME: not implemented: ... ; errors remain visible. Installed

artifacts created before version metadata was recorded show an unknown app

version until the APK is installed again.

Use --trace launch,runtime,ui,click before the APK or command for startup,

items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.content:
The real-life risks of relying on proprietary software

Google has announced that schools refusing to subject their students to its so-called artificial intelligence will also lose access to Google Search. Strong-arming schools into using machine learning systems — at the expense of a student's learning — is drawing the attention of teachers and parents. This outrage towards Google is justified, and this latest development is merely a symptom of a bigger problem: proprietary software does not belong in schools.

There was a time when staff at prestigious universities pushed back against the capture of student and teacher services by Google and Microsoft. This even resulted in boycotts of university email. A decade later, educational institutions from primary schools to colleges that had adopted proprietary software to replace their internal services are now finding themselves increasingly subject to the ups and downs — quite literally — of the companies that control their systems. Recently, Microsoft pulled email and other collaboration services from the gratis tier of its 365 Education suite, which is also undergoing broader pricing changes, including storage. Notably, " Each pupil on A0 has to actively use a Windows device for their learning ." The change has caused quite a stir in the UK education system as it could affect institutions' bills in serious ways.

The Free Software Foundation (FSF) has long warned that gratis proprietary software comes with a steep price tag: your freedom. Proprietary corporations offer their software as bait: "Take our software," they say. "Use our programs," they say. Meanwhile, years of student information, assignments, and email is stored in the so-called "cloud" and held hostage, making a change of services all the more challenging. These proprietary corporations chuckle to themselves as they lock educational institutions into their platforms, and then laugh again when they change the conditions. Proprietary software platforms for education stand in opposition to everything education should represent. Education is about helping students collaborate, investigate and solve problems, and develop deeper understanding. It prepares people for life and helps shape their personal values. Free software allows these skills to develop .

At present, student data is well protected in the education system in many countries, but do we really believe these corporations' intentions? These companies collect information over several years of students' lives — data of minors and maturing children, and historically far more than is necessary . Targeted data mining is what these companies do best. Surveillance is always troubling, but the argument of "protecting our children" is used all the time, often when it's a complete overreach. The argument is strong because we do want to make sure they are safe. Students spend so much of their time at school developing into the human beings that we need them to become. We owe our youth the best we can offer them in education and privacy.

The real-life risks of relying on proprietary providers for essential services are all over the news. This week, the world came to a crashing halt in several ways, with Microsoft , banks , air travel , the NSA , and Apple all disrupted, affecting countless people globally. Four major disruptions in four consecutive days. We have put a lot of eggs in very few so-called baskets, and the cracks are showing .

Our society is trapped in the belief that large and visible corporations have everything under control — that their software is somehow the better, safer, or more reliable choice simply because it is paid and proprietary. People place their entire digital lives in the hands of a company providing a false sense of safety. But make no mistake: there is no superiority in software from Big Tech, as none of the mentioned attributes have any causal relation to each other. Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading

The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .

South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. items.title: Valkey: From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient
items.content:
A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.

In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree .

fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops.

In a 5-million-member test, it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36–43%, saving up to 109 MB.

Let's take a look at why this change happened and how it works.

Large sorted sets that exceed the listpack threshold are backed by a skiplist paired with a hashtable (smaller sorted sets use a compact listpack representation that stores elements sequentially in contiguous memory).

The hashtable gives O(1) lookups by member, while the skiplist gives O(log n) ordered lookups by rank or score.

That pairing is architecturally simple, but the skiplist carries a significant memory cost.

It stores exactly one element per node, scattered across memory as separate allocations connected by pointers.

Valkey's skiplist pays for this in raw memory.

Every node carries a backward pointer (8B), plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, since skiplists are probabilistic (each node has a 25% chance of gaining another level).

Each level costs 8B for the pointer plus 8B for the span value, giving around 29B of pointer and span overhead per node.

Add the 8B score, and the total reaches roughly 37B per node before accounting for the member string.

Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of hardware caches (L1, L2, and L3) to keep frequently accessed data close to the processor.

These caches are much smaller and faster than main memory (RAM), so when the CPU cannot find the data it needs in its cache, it must fetch it from a slower level of the memory hierarchy.

As a rough illustration, an L1 cache hit can take about 1 ns, while a DRAM access can take around 100 ns.

A dependent memory access can leave the core waiting; actual latency and how much work can be hidden vary by system and workload 1 .

Each node in the skiplist is a separate allocation, potentially scattered wherever the heap happened to place it, so following the structure can require repeatedly fetching data from unrelated memory locations.

Because each step can determine where the next step goes, these fetches are dependent, resulting in more round trips through the memory hierarchy.

A 2025 study of concurrent in-memory indexes found that, on its tested workloads, traditional skiplists experienced roughly 2.4–4.8× more cache misses than a comparable B-tree, with 2–8× lower throughput 2 (testing different data structure implementations, not Valkey).

A B+ tree keeps entries sorted in fixed-size nodes: leaf nodes hold the entries, or pointers to them, and inner nodes hold just enough routing data to pick which child to descend into.

Packing many entries into each node addresses both problems above: far less per-member pointer overhead, and far fewer dependent fetches per lookup.

fbtree, short for Feature B+ Tree, uses a 61-way fanout: each node can hold up to 61 entries or child pointers.

Leaf and inner nodes are sized to fit jemalloc allocation classes without wasting space on 64-bit builds; on supported 32-bit builds, innerNode is rounded up to the 1280-byte class.

A 512-byte leaf holds up to 61 value pointers, so 61 members share one node instead of each getting its own.

Instead of storing the score and member separately, fbtree stores them together as a single packed value: the normalized 8-byte score followed by the member bytes.

This keeps the data needed for comparisons together and removes another level of pointer indirection.

The skiplist's 25%-per-level rule gives it an effective branching factor of about 4, while fbtree's fanout is 61.

items.title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
items.content:
“… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859

[ Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.]

I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven . I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis , producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code .

At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line ( Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?

For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem ), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.

David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.

Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!

All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.

Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean.  They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves.  And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds.  And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?

My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.

The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will…

items.title: Visited links are purple
items.content:
A few weeks ago Kev Quirk asked: Do you use :visited on links? — and I said to myself: No! I don’t use visited links… but why don’t I use visited links?

TL;DR: I’ve gone and styled visited links, and they’re purple.

I did a cursory five minutes of research and found Wikipedia still styles visited links (blue to purple). MDN does too. As does the GOV.UK design system — they have a special class to opt-out of the visited style. BBC News turns black links to grey, how emo.

I decided to style visited links within my <main> body copy. Which to be fair is most links but not the big headings on my blog index for example. I was too intimidated to turn those purple. Maybe you can give me the courage to style those too?

It looked a bit weird at first but I like the colourful additions to my blog.

WCAG 2.2 guidelines have no requirement to differentiate visited from unvisited links. Regardless, visited links should meet all the same criteria applied to any link.

There is one specific exception ( following this discussion ). Because web browsers have strict style limitations and technical constraints due to privacy concerns :

Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1.

This means that a subtle contrast different in blue vs purple is not considered an accessibility failure under that rule.

Web accessibility is all about ensuring a comparable experience for all users. Nothing can be perfectly accessible though. I think this small enhancement is fine, even if not everyone can see the difference. It’s a rare exception though. I’m conscious that too often excuses are made to ignore UX parity. I think any higher contrast or another visual indicator would be off-putting and impede readability. Forgoing any style doesn’t help anyone either. If blue and purple is good enough for those examples mentioned above, I’m on board.

Bryce Wray commented on Kev Quirk’s blog to note that Chromium browsers introduced :visited link partitioning in 2025. I had no idea this was a thing!

What do you think, do you care about visited link styles?

I found Kev Quirk’s blog on bubbles.town . Bubbles is a charming social RSS aggregator. It’s doing a great job at supporting small personal blogs and promoting non-toxic topics. Bubbles is far from perfect though. It probably needs a tech filter. It certainly needs more participation in comments and voting. The developer is actively working to improve the site and a community is growing, so that’s cool to see.

I hope Bubbles can thrive and remain human. This is the web we need to bypass the dead web Google et. al. are gatekeeping. Let them wall themselves in with their slop!

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
items.content:
Staffers at the Internet Archive , the nonprofit “ digital library ” that runs the Wayback Machine , are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996 . Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.

Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”

The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI .

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.)

Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”

Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.
