items.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
items.content:
Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations

This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and

T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026).

lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ).

lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2

and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper.

lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved.

The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in

place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each

comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree,

and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice .

The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and

The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the

paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by

a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through

FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository.

The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the

cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes

$(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics

of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the

conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

items.title: DreamCoder: coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
items.content:
It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called DreamCoder , an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

DreamCoder is a frontier coding harness with a tiling window manager that runs in your browser on all 3 platforms.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker , a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively , and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by…

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

Get the latest cybersecurity news, critical vulnerabilities, threat intelligence, tutorials, and exclusive giveaways delivered straight to your inbox. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

Meta confirmed the vulnerability, pushed an emergency patch Friday night, and clarified that no backend database was breached. That last part is technically accurate. It’s also somewhat beside the point.

To understand why this worked, you need to understand what Meta’s AI support assistant was authorized to do.

Instagram has notoriously poor human support infrastructure. Recovering a locked account – especially a high-value one can take weeks of back-and-forth with an automated ticketing system. Meta’s solution was to deploy a conversational AI layer to handle common recovery workflows: relinking a lost email address, triggering a password reset, verifying account ownership. In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”

The devices have their own web interface:

When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:

The script runs at night checking for an open door:

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you."

Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
items.content:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been.

Except in software engineering, somehow.

When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.”

Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.

To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills.

“There’s more to software engineering than writing code”

Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change.

Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you?

So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing!

All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems

if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-122230 📢 Source: Wordfence 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False The Thim Kit for Elementor – Pre-built Templates & Widgets for Elementor plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via the 'comment' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.4.8 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Exploitation requires that the Post Comment widget is used with the Text Reveal entrance animation (Elementor class 'ekit--fx-word-reveal') on a Single Post template, and the comment widget must be within the initial viewport; once the first comment by an attacker is approved, or if comment moderation is disabled, subsequent payloads fire automatically for every visitor who loads the affected page. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-21T09:31:04.629Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-122230
